etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bach, bache, bahche, from Old English *bæċċ (“something baked”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-West Germanic *bakku, from Proto-Germanic *bakkuz (“baking, baked goods”), cognate with Middle High German becke (“something baked, pastry, baking, bakery”). Related also to Old English bacan (“to bake”), Old English ġebæc (“something baked”), Dutch gebak, German Gebäck, Dutch baksel.

definitions.definition: The quantity of bread or other baked goods baked at one time.
(by extension) A quantity of anything produced at one operation.
A group or collection of things of the same kind, such as a batch of letters or the next batch of business.

quote.citation: c. 1710-1720, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, Epistle to Lord Hervey on the King's Birthday

definitions.definition: (computing) A set of data to be processed at one time.

quote.text: Except the baker doe his part also in the batch.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To aggregate things together into a batch.
(transitive, computing) To handle a set of input data or requests as a batch process.
Of a process, operating for a defined set of conditions, and then halting.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bache, bæcche, from Old English bæċ, beċe (“brook, stream”). Doublet of beck. More at beach.

definitions.definition: A field or patch of ground lying near a stream; the dale in which a stream flows.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Clipping of bachelor (“unmarried adult male”).

definitions.definition: (informal) To live as a bachelor temporarily, of a married man or someone virtually married.
